author: AfricanFeminism
title: Laws and Resurgent Cultural Claims: Rwanda’s Decency Policing Erodes Women’s Freedoms
content:
There’s been an online uproar after Rwandan National Police spokesperson ACP Rutikanga Boniface announced on public television that public indecency will be punished. On August 29, police officers threatened to beat young women attending a concert by Tanzanian singer Diamond Platnumz if they did not follow the new ‘decency’ orders.


In Rubavu, a town in the west of the country, a young woman was seen on video being apprehended by police over the length of her dress. Thereafter, several government workers using the X platform stated that it is important for Rwandan culture to be upheld and that the ‘Western ways’ used to sexualize women’s bodies through revealing clothing are corrupting the youth. These are not isolated incidents.


Women’s bodies and the rights of gender-expansive and marginalized people have increasingly become battlegrounds for Christian fundamentalist moralists and lobbyists.


Rwandan law does not clearly define indecency.

Article 143 of Law N° 68/2018 states: “Any person who performs an indecent act in public commits an offence.” Conviction can lead to imprisonment for six months to two years.

 In 2023, there were discussions about redefining indecency as “showing one’s private parts or performing sexual acts in public,” but this was not adopted. Ambiguity remains over what constitute

s a ‘private part,’ making enforcement unclear and subjective. This also opens the door to bias against women and girls, as body parts like shoulders or cleavage may be deemed indecent, similar to theocratic states treating exposed hair as indecent.


Social media is flooded with calls for clarity on the law, as its guidelines would be replicated at entrances to businesses, hotels, and restaurants. This demonstrates how legal ambiguity fuels public scrutiny and the policing of women and girls. Women are speaking up about how legal definitions of decency affect their lives. We cannot live in a world where a mere body can incriminate a person, or where enforcers arbitrarily decide what clothing is

 inappropriate

.


This debate is feeding into an already pervasive culture of gender-based violence whose victims are disproportionately women, girls and gender expansive people. Technology Facilitated Gender Based Violence (TFGBV), already common, is being fueled on TikTok and Instagram, where several young men and some journalists are justifying rape as the woman or girl’s fault due to what she is wearing.


On September 2, a young woman in Kibagabaga was harassed, beaten, undressed, and insulted by a group of men. The video has circulated on social media, but the perpetrators remain unpunished, and the girl’s fate is unknown. Now, online platforms—driven by manosphere communities and technocapitalists profiting from dehumanization—have become battlegrounds for controlling women’s public and private lives.


Mob violence and GBV have been normalized as of late, and public institutions have remained silent. Rwandan women and girls feel ignored, helpless, and abandoned.


The Ministry of Gender and Family Promotion, whose mandate is to champion gender equality, has in the past

 implicitly responded

to rising rates of teenage pregnancies by blaming parents and

mothers for failing to raise ‘decent’ girls

. Once again, the risk in this

rhetoric

is that women, girls, and gender-expansive people become blamed for such deeply rooted systems of inequality and oppression. Subjective matters such as manners, morals, hemline lengths, and even treating nudity as indecency are regressions rooted in colonial and religious control of African bodies.


Counting Women, Not Counting on Rights


All this is happening while women hold 64 percent of seats in parliament, yet they are not fighting against the resurgent social control of women’s bodies or the legal silences that enable it. Rwanda has had a parliamentary women’s majority for nearly two decades, yet this has not resulted in real change, as patriarchal control of women’s lives continues to resurface.


On August 7, 2022, police arrested 24-year-old Liliane Mugabekazi after a photo of her at a concert taken by a journalist circulated online. She was charged with public indecency under Article 143 and faced imprisonment. Prosecutors claimed her clothing “revealed her private parts”—her breasts. A Kicukiro Primary Court judge initially denied her bail. Mugabekazi pleaded not guilty, noting she did not take or share the photo and had passed venue security. She was later …

author: ROAPE
title: African migrant workers who cannot return
content:
Somebody in Kampala or Accra or Harare sees a job advertisement. Customer service, or something in IT, somewhere abroad. The pay is better than anything available at home. The recruiter is responsive and reassuring. A ticket arrives.


That is where most accounts of migrant labour abuse begin, and it is worth sitting with how ordinary it sounds. Nobody in that story is reckless. They are doing what people have always done when opportunity is scarce, which is to go where the work is.


What happens next is the part that does not make the news often enough.


The scale is global, not exclusively African.

UNODC, citing INTERPOL, reports

 that people from 66 countries across every continent have been trafficked into online scam centres, with 74 per cent of identified victims brought to centres in Southeast Asia. African workers are therefore one part of a much wider labour pool. Their experience still deserves particular attention because, as the cases below show, rescue does not end the problem when consular support and repatriation capacity are uneven.


The mechanism that makes everything else possible


Across the Gulf, Jordan and Lebanon, migrant workers live under a

sponsorship regime

 that ties a person’s legal right to remain in the country to one specific employer. That employer can, in practice, determine whether the worker changes jobs, and in some cases whether they can leave the country at all.


It is lawful and it is routine, which is precisely why it deserves more attention than it gets. It does not require anybody to break the law to produce misery. It only requires an employer willing to use the leverage the system hands them. The result is a worker who cannot walk away, and once a person cannot walk away, everything else becomes negotiable: their wages, their hours, their passport, their safety.


The most extreme version of that principle is not lawful at all. Along the Thai border near Myawaddy, and in Shan State near the Chinese frontier, thousands of people are held in fortified compounds and forced to conduct online fraud for transnational criminal networks, targeting victims around the world through investment, romance, cryptocurrency and other scams.


A

United Nations report

 published earlier this year documented what that involves: torture and other ill-treatment, sexual abuse, forced abortions, food deprivation and solitary confinement. Survivors interviewed for it came from Ghana, South Africa and Zimbabwe, among other countries. One man from Ghana described being made to watch a friend beaten in front of him.


The legal system and the criminal one are not equivalent, and nobody serious claims they are. But they run on the same principle: take away a person’s ability to leave, and there is very little they can refuse.


Rescue is not the same as return


There is a further problem that receives almost no attention. Crackdowns can close individual sites without dismantling the wider networks, which have

repeatedly adapted, relocated or expanded elsewhere

. And the people pulled out of them are frequently left in limbo.


Reuters reported in March 2025

 that nearly 7,000 people rescued from scam centres in Myanmar were awaiting repatriation through Thailand, including Chinese, Indonesian and African nationals. Some remained in militia-run border camps facing food shortages, limited medical care and no means to pay for the journey home. That imbalance matters: rescue can happen in one day, while return depends on documentation, diplomatic coordination and a government able to act for its citizens.


This is what makes consular capacity a human rights issue rather than an administrative one. Being rescued and being home are two different things, and the gap between them is measured in whose government showed up.


Saad Kassis-Mohamed has spent years arguing that these are not isolated tragedies but predictable outcomes of systems working as designed. His advocacy has focused on migrant-worker protection, humanitarian action, climate justice and social equality, and on a demand that sounds modest until you try to enforce it: that reforms should be judged by whether anything actually improved for the people they were written for.


He develops that argument further in

The Kafala System

, prepared by Saad Kassis-Mohamed Center, which examines sponsorship-based dependency in the Gulf and Lebanon before extending the analysis to trafficking and forced criminality in Myanmar. The Center …

author: Christopher Rutledge
title: Free speech is not freedom from facts
content:
A strange thing happens to a claim when it moves from a WhatsApp group or a Facebook post into a radio studio. It changes its clothes.


What begins as a rumour on social media can sound very different once it enters a national broadcaster’s studio. The familiar presenter, the recognised station, the rituals of a professional interview, and the authority of being on air all lend the claim credibility it didn’t have before. The listener is no longer hearing merely what someone said online; they are hearing it through an institution they have been taught to trust, and it is easy to assume that if it has reached the microphone, someone must have checked whether it is true.


That is why the recent Broadcasting Complaints Commission of South Africa

(BCCSA) ruling against SAFM

 matters. It is also why some of the criticism of the ruling misses the point.


After SAFM broadcast the apology ordered by the BCCSA, some people asked whether organisations such as Macua (Mining Affected Communities United in Action) were now deciding what could and could not be said in the media. Others suggested that this amounted to controlling the narrative or restricting free speech.


It sounds like a reasonable concern. Nobody should want civil society, government, business or any political organisation to decide which opinions South Africans are permitted to hear.


But that is not what happened here.


We did not ask SAFM to stop interviewing Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, nor did we ask the broadcaster to ban March and March, nor did we ask that controversial views about immigration be removed from the public conversation.


What we were asking was fairly basic: if a claim is presented as fact, particularly on a national broadcaster, the audience is entitled to know what it rests on and whether it can be verified.


The lie about immigrants and crime


Ngobese-Zuma told SAFM listeners that foreign nationals were responsible for 60% of serious crime in Gauteng… Read that sentence again. Not that she believed migrants were contributing to crime. Not that immigration was, in her view, badly managed. She gave a figure: 60%.


A number sounds precise; it sounds researched and official. Once such a number is repeated on national radio, it begins to circulate.


People repeat it at work. Someone forwards it to a WhatsApp family group. A politician quotes it. A Facebook post appears, saying, ‘Even the radio said foreigners commit 60% of crime’.


Soon, nobody remembers where the figure began. They only remember the figure.


However, when the claim was examined, the evidence failed to support it.


GroundUp


and the

Institute for Security Studies

 investigated the broader claims about migrants and serious crime and found no evidence that foreign nationals account for anything approaching such a share of serious crime. Even the prison statistics commonly invoked in these debates do not tell the story people imagine: a significant proportion of foreign nationals in prison are there for immigration-related offences, not the violent crimes usually implied.


And this is the crucial point: saying that a police officer mentioned a figure does not magically make it a reliable statistic, especially since it has been debunked numerous times.


Anti-immigrant, ‘peaceful’ protesters in Alexandra, Johannesburg, carrying weapons and some covering their faces. File photo by Simon Ramapuputla


The BCCSA found that SAFM failed to inquire about the claim’s origins. The commissioner noted that the presenter neither endorsed the 60% claim nor challenged it, leaving listeners to accept it.


That is the distinction between censorship and journalism. Censorship says: you may not say that. Journalism says: you have said it; now show us why we should believe you.


The lie about foreign military bases


The distinction matters because the 60% claim was not the only one. Listeners were also told about foreign military bases allegedly operating in South Africa. They heard allegations that NGOs receiving foreign funding were buying weapons. There were claims that explosives were entering the country and that foreigners were paying police officers.


Again, these are not vague political opinions. Either the military bases exist or they do not. Either particular NGOs are buying weapons or they are not. Either there is evidence of a widespread system in which migrants bribe police officers or there is not.


When

GroundUp

 examined some of these claims, the picture began …

author: WoMin
title: Wathint’ Abafazi, Wathint’ Imbokodo: Why Challenging Xenophobia Is Unfinished Women’s Business
content:
On 17 August, SADC leaders concluded their 46th summit in Durban, against a backdrop of heightened xenophobic protests, threats, and forced repatriations. August is Women’s Month in South Africa commemorating 70 years since women marched on the Union Buildings fighting against apartheid and pass laws. However, this month has been marred by the recent spate of Afrophobia and xenophobia across the country. SADC’s communiqué recorded an update from South Africa on migration governance and called for coordinated regional dialogue on the drivers of migration. It did not explicitly name xenophobia or Afrophobia — even after months in which Black African migrants have faced intimidation, violence, and pressure to leave South Africa. In an 

Open Letter

 to the SADC Heads of State and Government, WoMin African Alliance, together with The People’s Dialogue, calls for those Heads of State to place xenophobia and Afrophobia in South Africa on its formal agenda, issue a clear public resolution, and commit to measurable regional action. 


Those 20 000 courageous women across race, class and religion marched on 9 August 1956 to confront the Apartheid regime’s institutionalisation of white supremacy and racial capitalism by controlling Black life and movement. The Pass Laws inscribed that control, requiring pass books at all times, and described Black people as “aliens” and “illegal” in the country of their birth. Sophie De Bruyn, the only living leader at this year’s commemoration, shared “that the freedom we marched and bled for is in reality a painful paradox. How can we celebrate our past victories when our current realities are so deeply disappointing and distressful?”  


The pass laws did not simply restrict movement — they dictated who belonged where, who could work, where they could live, and who counted as fully human within South Africa’s borders.  


This historic day of protest was about fighting for a free, democratic South Africa in which all peoples, regardless of race, class and gender, could be emancipated and live with dignity and equality. Already liberated countries on the continent stood alongside Black South Africans in full solidarity, offering a home, bearing the brunt of economic pressure and military assault, especially for frontline states.  


While the pass laws are painful history, the current reality for Black South Africans falls far short of our freedom dreams. Much of Apartheid endures in lived memory — continued spatial injustice, the deepest economic inequality globally, and more than 33.6% unemployment. 


For WoMin African Alliance, rooted in Pan African feminist politics, this is no coincidence. Women’s Month cannot be commemorated as mere nostalgia — it must be treated as unfinished business. The emergence of Xenophobia and Afrophobia results from deep, intersecting crises in South Africa, as set out in our 

statement

 on Afrophobia and Xenophobia. 


The root cause of this crisis is the neoliberal economic policies implemented by the South African government, along with a long history of racial capitalism in which Black people were exploited for cheap labour to build the economy but have remained economically and politically excluded. What we are witnessing is the crumbling and disintegration of our society. Today, South Africa’s huge unemployment rate represents millions of lives suspended in a state of permanent insecurity. This disintegration has the greatest impact and consequences on Black women. 


Impacts on women

 


Women face the most inequality, earning 23% to 35% less than men for the same work, and accounted for 77% of all job losses in 2025. They are concentrated in low-income, informal, or precarious employment such as domestic work. Women-headed households face a roughly 60% chance of being poor. This places a triple burden on women, who bear most unpaid domestic work and child-rearing — labour unrecognised in national accounts and that hampers their economic advancement. 


These statistics represent structural violence rooted in inequality, patriarchy, social dislocation, and dispossession. Rather than confront the state’s failure to transform the economy and property relations, create decent work, or provide basic services, migrants become easy scapegoats for crises produced by capitalist and neoliberal policy. The unemployed South African is encouraged to blame the Zimbabwean street vendor, the Ethiopian spaza shop owner, or the Somali trader, instead of asking why …

author: Gathanga Ndung’u
title: This book was born in the streets
content:
Often, history is written as a recollection of the past. It is treated as the entry of passive data, only to be archived for posterity. But what happens when history, or its making, runs parallel to its archival process?

This is the opportunity offered by the

2024–2025 youth uprisings

 in Kenya. They gave us room to make history, to analyze events as they unfolded daily, and to document them at the same time. However, proper analysis and recourse were insufficient to help tilt the scale from the state to the masses.

Nevertheless, the documentation of the contestations between the masses and the machinery of the state has been extensive. They have been documented in music, memes, spoken word, poems, graffiti, murals, and essays such as our recent scrapbook titled

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

.

As a contribution to the struggle,

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

 collects essays from an intergenerational tapestry of activists, community organizers, writers, and legal minds. It is a conversation between the old and the new, produced in the trenches of the youth uprisings, forging an intergenerational continuum of resistance.

The question of sovereignty appears in all the discussions in

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

. From the streets to the book, external interference in the country’s affairs has been a constant reminder of the incomplete independence we gained in 1963.

One of the book’s main sovereignty concerns stems from the role of multilateral lending institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Some contributors have also analyzed this very question by focusing on the rising foreign military “partnerships” with countries such as the UK, which runs the oldest foreign military unit in Kenya,

the British Army Training Unit Kenya (BATUK)

, which was set up at independence in 1964. Similarly, the US operates

Camp Simba

 and Manda Bay Airfield, and Emmanuel Macron is the new entrant in these defense “cooperations”; his government signed a

defense and security partnership

 with the Kenyan government, which saw 800 French troops visit Mombasa in May 2026 for an exercise under the agreement.

The book also looks at ongoing cooperation between different Kenyan police units with the

Israeli state

, which is known for gross violations of human rights. Israel continues to equip the Kenyan police with further skills and technology to enable extensive monitoring of protestors, activists, community organizers, and journalists who are considered dissidents.

We also discuss the

Seed and Plant Varieties Act of 2022

, which sought to criminalize the saving, sharing, and exchanging of uncertified seeds. For many across the country, this was seen as a takeover of our food system. Labeling indigenous seeds and cultivars as uncertified would have made way for agricultural corporations to create a monopoly on the seed market, giving them a firm grip on our food system. Thankfully, through organizing,

the act was defeated in November 2025

, when the High Court of Kenya in Machakos declared sections of the act unconstitutional.

From the publishing of the book to the launch, we have had our fair share of challenges. The process has been full of fear, tension, and intimidation, but also one full of courage and determination. After months compiling our voices through the essays, proofreading and editing, the manuscript was ready for publishing. Kenya, being a nation with a considerable size of progressive forces and some level of political freedom, we never anticipated that the book would be “too hot a potato to handle” for most publishing houses. The title scared every potential publisher in the country, comrades, and even some safe spaces that we initially thought could provide a home for the book.

We got many suggestions from different quarters to revise the manuscript title to

From Mau Mau to Gen Zs

. Various justifications were given for why it was a bad idea to proceed with the current title. Some saw it as a way of exposing ourselves too much, while others felt the state might misinterpret the title. As a contributor and one of the people who were involved in its various processes, I knew that the title came with its fair share of risks and burdens to shoulder, but we were all ready for it. To us, “Ruto Must Go” was not just a slogan or a fleeting chant, but a movement that understood what Ruto or Rutoism represented. “Ruto Must Go” meant death to the system whose image is mirrored …

author: Goktug Caliskan
title: How much is a human worth? Nigeria’s growing kidnapping economy
content:
On 21 August, armed men entered a mosque in 

Dekara village

 in Niger State while Friday prayers were underway. At around the same time, nearby settlements were also raided. A few days later, a 

video circulated

 on social media showing hundreds of people, including women, children and elderly people, sitting on the ground in a wooded area. One of the armed men addressed their families, asking them to identify their relatives in the footage.


The exact number of people abducted remains unclear. Local residents say the figure is 

around 600

. At least 

30 people

were killed in the aftermath of the attack, while around 2,000 others crossed the border 

into Benin

. The Nigerian government launched a large-scale 

rescue operation

 involving the military, police and intelligence services.


New figures released immediately after the incident showed that what happened in Dekara was far from exceptional. Between July 2025 and June 2026, 

7,825 people

 were kidnapped in Nigeria. That represents a 66 percent increase compared with the previous period. During the same period, at least 

1,142 people

 were killed, while the confirmed amount of ransom paid by families to kidnappers reached 7.78 billion naira, or approximately 

$5.8 million

.


At first glance, this looks like a severe security problem. A closer look reveals something else. Kidnapping in Nigeria is moving beyond a fragmented activity in which individual criminals extort money and is turning into 

an economy

 with its own financing, bargaining system, target selection and expectation of recurring revenue.


The price of a human being is also determined through bargaining in this economy.


The economics of mass abduction


It is impossible to attribute all kidnappings in Nigeria to a single organization. In the northeast, Boko Haram and groups linked to ISIS remain active. In the northwest and central parts of the country, heavily armed criminal networks locally referred to as bandits attack villages, roads and schools. In some areas, the boundaries between these two worlds are becoming increasingly blurred.


In the past, kidnapping was often a more selective crime targeting a particular businessman, politician or wealthy family. Today, mass abductions are becoming increasingly prominent. According to data from the past year, around 80 percent of victims were taken in attacks carried out against 

groups of people

.


The economic logic behind this is fairly straightforward. A single raid on a village or school can result in dozens, sometimes hundreds, of people being captured. Negotiations can then be conducted with the hostages’ families and communities. Even if the amount obtained from each individual remains relatively low, total revenue rises rapidly as the number of hostages increases.


The cost for the attackers is also relatively limited. An armed group enters a remote settlement where state presence is weak, takes people into forested areas and can hold them there for weeks or even months. Vast forests that security forces struggle to reach, poor roads and porous borders make this easier.


This is why a human being in Nigeria today has almost become a mobile financial asset. From the kidnappers’ perspective, a hostage’s family income, profession, place of residence or the fundraising capacity of their community can influence the course of negotiations.


The limits of the ransom ban


Nigeria faces an extremely difficult dilemma. Paying ransom 

is illegal

. The logic is understandable. As long as money continues to be paid, kidnapping remains profitable, and every successful negotiation becomes a source of financing for the next attack.


Yet it is much harder to tell a mother or father whose child is being held in a forest not to pay because doing so finances the criminal economy.


Families often do not know when a rescue operation will begin or whether it will succeed. Hostages can be held for weeks under the threat of hunger, disease and violence.


In such circumstances, economic theory loses its meaning for a family. Selling a house, livestock, farmland or any other possession in an attempt to buy back the life of a loved one becomes understandable for many people.


When a family pays ransom and saves its child, it may have done what it considers the right thing. But when that money is converted into weapons, motorcycles, fuel, food or new recruits, the capital for the next kidnapping is created.


A government ban alone …

author: Hassan Alnaser, Mohamed Alagra, Mashair Idris, Ehsan Salah
title: Sudan Nashra: US push to expand arms embargo to all of Sudan at UNSC postponed at last minute | Amid unprecedented arms build-up at RSF base in Ethiopia, Burhan, Isaias probe elusive mutual guarantees | Tasis’s unified general command to be led by Abdel Rahim Dagalo, sources say | Quintet meets domestic dialogue’s preparatory committee on Khartoum visit, source says
content:
Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter


here

.


After days of fierce lobbying in New York, the United States backed away on Thursday from a vote at the United Nations Security Council on a sweeping arms embargo covering all of Sudan.


Washington had spent the preceding hours trying to line up nine votes to pass the resolution while working to keep Russia and China from vetoing it, according to four UN sources, an Arab diplomat, two Sudanese diplomats and a Sudanese former diplomatic advisor who spoke to Mada Masr in the leadup to the vote. But by Thursday, the Americans had concluded that putting the draft as it is to a vote would end with a Russian veto, one of the UN sources told Mada Masr.


The US resolution would replace the current Darfur embargo, which expires on September 12. The proposal brings weapons supplied to all parties to the war, including the Sudanese military, under international restrictions. That would include drones and related technologies, which have come to dominate the fighting.


The Security Council is now expected to vote on a rollover of the existing sanctions for one month, during which the US would try to lobby members and negotiate changes to its proposal on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in late September, a second UN source said.


The diplomatic battle over the embargo is playing out alongside a war that continues to draw in outside powers and take on a broader regional dimension. With states on both sides stepping in to shore up their respective allies, attention has recently shifted to Ethiopia, where an unprecedented arms buildup has been observed at the Ethiopian Asosa base used by the Rapid Support Forces and its allies to operate an increasingly critical front in the Sudanese Blue Nile.


The buildup comes as Ethiopia’s internal conflict is threatening to boil over and its tensions with Eritrea rise, creating a fast-approaching possibility of several conflicts converging along Sudan’s eastern border. That was the backdrop of Transitional Sovereignty Council Chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan September 4 visit to Asmara, where he met Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki.


An Eritrean security source informed of the talks told Mada Masr that the two leaders discussed how to prevent Sudan’s war from spilling into Eritrea. Asmara wants a clearer picture of how eastern Sudan and the border areas are being used, particularly as the Sudan-Ethiopia border is a point of overlap between Sudan’s war and Ethiopia’s internal conflict.


Neither side was ready, however, to say what it would do if that overlap develops into a broader regional confrontation, despite the meeting being about working out where the other might stand, according to the source.


For now, Sudan and Eritrea have agreed to maintain high-level coordination and information sharing, according to the source and a Sudanese political source.


Within Sudan, the RSF is trying to give its political project a more institutional face and enough weight to avoid being sidelined from diplomacy around the war.


Over five days in Nyala, the capital of the RSF-led parallel government, Tasis’s leadership body agreed to complete and activate the government’s institutions and form a “national military.” What was left unannounced last week though was that RSF Deputy Commander Abdel Rahim Dagalo has been selected to head the unified general command, according to a source close to him and a Tasis official.


The arrangement gives Tasis a clearer division between its political and military leadership. Abdel Rahim would head the military institution while Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo remains commander of the RSF and heads Tasis’s political institutions, the two sources said.


But bringing forces that entered the war from different positions, with their own commanders and military traditions, under one command will be a highly complex process. Doing that while those forces are fighting on multiple fronts is a delicate balancing act.


The risks of that balancing act are already evident within the alliance’s main military and political partner, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North led by Abdel Aziz al-Hilu. The group is facing growing resentment and violent pushback to what some of its constituencies see as the leadership’s increasingly blurred position inside Tasis, a leadership figure in the SPLM-N said. Establishing a unified command under Abdel Rahim without resolving those tensions could alienate the constituencies …

author: By Andrew Lee, Contributor
title: Activist Blogging Platform Shuts Down After Terrorism Designation
content:
Washington D.C. — On August 26, 2026, the U.S. Departments of State and the Treasury

designated

 a volunteer tech collective behind a popular activist blogging platform a terrorist organization. 


Autistici/Inventati (A/I), the Italian collective behind

NoBlogs.org

, now

joins

 such organizations as the Islamic State group and al Qaeda on the list of Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs), a category created by former President George W. Bush in an

executive order

 weeks after the 9/11 attacks. Shortly thereafter, Autistici/Inventati lost their domain, autistici.org, and had their Italian

bank account closed

 due to the threat of US sanctions. 


NoBlogs was

hacked

 on August 28th, two days after the terrorism designation. A “Free Palestine” button on the NoBlogs homepage was redirected to link to a US government “self deportation” site, and a message was

posted

 claiming that NoBlogs user information had been “saved and given to the United States government.” The hack was

quickly promoted

 on X by right-wing influencer and Pentagon employee Jennica Pounds. On September 6th, Autistici/Inventati

announced

 its imminent closure. 


A/I, which provided its services such as NoBlogs to protect activists, feared that maintaining its services would only expose users to additional risk given the “political climate” now that it was labeled a Specially Designated Global Terrorist. 


“Under these circumstances, we are no longer able to maintain our original mission – offering secure and non-commercial digital tools,” explained the collective in a

statement

. “Now turn off your PCs, get out of your homes, struggle, hug each other and keep on smiling. We are stopping, but the Resistance and ideas do not stop. Stay human.” In an announcement on

September 8th

, A/I reported that emails, listservs, and NoBlogs accounts would cease operation within the following ten days. 


May First Movement Technology, a nonprofit that similarly provides internet services for social movement groups, released a statement that “emphatically condemns” the A/I sanctions, which it called “excessive and vindictive.” May First had one of its former members, Samidoun Palestinian Prisoner Solidarity Network, likewise designated as a terrorist group by the Treasury Department in 2024. “US government can effectively isolate any organization without presenting evidence or trial,” May First

stated

, “by simply alleging that they support terrorism.”


“From what we understand,” an A/I member had stated in an

Italian-language interview

, “any American citizen who interacts with us after [a US Treasury Department

deadline

 of] September 25 would risk 30 years in jail.”

Executive Order 13244

 bans the “making or receiving of any contribution of funds, goods, or services to or for the benefit of” Specially Designated Terrorist Groups. Designated Groups are “cut off” from the

U.S. financial system

, with all financial transactions blocked in areas subject to US law. Significantly, the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Asset Control reserves the right to levy

secondary sanctions

 against non-U.S. individuals, organizations, or financial institutions that have dealings with SDTGs. A/I’s Italian bank therefore faced the possibility of being itself blocked from the US financial system were it to continue providing banking services to the collective. 


“The real coercive power of the United States lies in progressively making it impossible to bank, host, or provide services to the designated entity,”

said

 Beniamino Irdi of the German Marshall Fund, a U.S. organization promoting transatlantic relations. “The power of sanctions derives from the ability to influence third parties, financial and commercial operators that, for compliance reasons, may decide to sever relations with the designated entity.”


Specially Designated Global Terrorists are distinct from Foreign Terrorist Organizations, which the powerful Atlantic Council think tank

refers to

 as the “gold standard of terrorism sanctions.” 


Former

Biden administration

 Senior Director for International Economics Peter Harrell contended in a

post on X

 that sanctions against A/I might be illegal under U.S. law, given the existence of a carve-out for “any postal, telegraphic, telephonic, or other personal communication” in the Berman Amendments to the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act. A legal challenge to A/I sanctions could have amounted to a …

author: Daron Letts
title: Inuit-owned companies seek private capital in Toronto
content:
Billions of dollars for infrastructure were on the menu at a Toronto luncheon hosted by the Government of Nunavut and Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. on Monday.


They organized the 90-minute event to coincide with the federal government’s inaugural Canada Investment Summit. The initiative

brought together Inuit, territorial, private and federal investment leaders to huddle over the territory’s major infrastructure projects that need financial backers.


The two-day summit, hosted by Prime Minister Mark Carney, is billed as one step in a five-year plan to attract $1 trillion in investment over the next five years.


“Our message is pretty clear right across all of these projects,” said West Kitikmeot Resources Corp. CEO Brendan Bell, in a phone interview on Monday.

“We’re going to need private capital to step up if these projects are going to become a reality.”


The Inuit-owned company Bell represents is looking for funders for its proposed $1-billion Gray’s Bay Port and Road project, which features a proposed 230-kilometre all-season road and Arctic deepsea port.


In March, that project was referred to the federal government’s new Major Projects Office, a special operating agency supported by the Privy Council Office with the goal of advancing nation-building projects.


“If not now, never,” he said of the project’s funding timeline.

“It’s about to get very serious.”


Inuit organizations and their networks cannot go it alone, he said.


Bell and other Arctic industry leaders remain optimistic, in part due to the rising profile of the Arctic on the global stage.


“The attention is very palpable on the Arctic,” said Nukik Corp. CEO Anne-Raphaëlle Audouin.

“That is progress because for many years we would have to really fight our way into those discussions, and sometimes to no avail. That has changed.”


The Inuit-owned company Audouin leads is heading another $1 billion infrastructure venture in its Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre project, scheduled to break ground in 2028, with final commissioning in 2032.


That project is part of the federal government’s Transmission InterConnect Investment Strategy.


The program seeks to meet the country’s growing electricity demand, estimated to double by 2050, while embracing Canada’s future net-zero emissions goal.


That national program, including the Kivalliq project, came online as part of the Major Projects Office in May.


For Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp. project director Keith Drover, this week’s networking opportunities have offered a chance to shore up existing relationships.


“So far it’s been revisiting strong connections within Canada,” he said. “We’ve had strong discussions

with

different groups.”


The Nunavut Nukkiksautiit Corp. subsidiary Drover is seeking support for the $750 million Iqaluit Nukkiksautiit Project.


The proposed

15-30 megawatt

 hydropower plant along the Kuugaluk River, about 60

km

 northeast of Iqaluit, is expected to replace an estimated 15 million litres of diesel that’s burned to generate electricity each year.


It was added to the major projects list in November 2025.


Arctic Economic Development Corp. vice-president of partnerships Jeffrey Ungalaq Maurice met with representatives from RBC and CIBC during the luncheon.


He pitched investment in the $350 million Qikiqtarjuaq Deep Sea Port.


Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations Rebecca Alty, the premiers of Northwest Territories and Yukon, and hosts Premier John Main and Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. vice-president Paul Irngaut also attended.

author: Amy Goodman
title: Broken Ceasefire Between Saudi Arabia and Houthis Could Renew Full War in Yemen
content:
“This ceasefire has been in place since 2022, but it has not ended the war in Yemen,” says professor Shireen Al-Adeimi.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Yemen is at risk of spiraling back into all-out war as Houthi forces and Saudi Arabia exchange new strikes amid a fight over control of the key Bab el-Mandeb strait through which much of Saudi oil passes on its way to world markets. The Houthis, the Iran-allied force also known as Ansarallah, has seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline from the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. The United Nations says the latest escalation has displaced 86,000 people in Yemen as the U.S. war on Iran continues to wrack the Middle East and raise oil prices around the world.

“What’s happening right now is essentially a break in the ceasefire between Ansarallah … and Saudi Arabia,” says Shireen Al-Adeimi, a Yemeni American associate professor at Michigan State University. “This ceasefire has been in place since 2022, but it has not ended the war in Yemen.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, Democracynow.org, the War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman.

Fear is growing — Yemen spiraling back into all-out war as Houthi forces and Saudi Arabia exchange new strikes. Earlier today, the Houthis claim to have launched a drone and missile strike on a military base in southern Saudi Arabia. This comes after the Houthis, who are aligned with Iran, seized Yemen’s entire Red Sea coastline including the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The area had been controlled by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. In recent days, Saudi Arabia has repeatedly launched airstrikes in Yemen in an effort to stall the Houthi advance. The U.N. says the latest escalation has displaced 86,000 people in Yemen. This all comes as Saudi Arabia shut down its major east-west pipeline after a drone strike launched from inside Iraq. It moves about 4% to 5% of the world’s global supply, oil supply.

To look at the escalating tensions between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, we go now to Shireen Al Adeimi, an associate professor at Michigan State University. Professor, thanks so much for being with us. Can you explain what’s happening right now in Yemen and the relationship between Yemen and Saudi Arabia as it relates to the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran?

SHIREEN AL-ADEIMI: Thanks so much for having me. What is happening right now is essentially a break in the ceasefire between Ansar Allah, who are known as the Houthis, and Saudi Arabia. The ceasefire has been in place since 2022 but it has not ended the war in Yemen. As you know, Yemen has been under a blockade by the Saudi forces, of course fully backed by the United States — the fourth administration now in the United States that’s been supporting the Saudis and has devastated Yemen. They had a bombing campaign that lasted for eight years and the blockade has not been fully lifted. So even though flights were operating in and out of Sanaa Airport, it was limited by Saudi Arabia to one flight a week, and everything coming in and out of the country still went through Saudi Arabia. Essentially, the blockade was still in place.

In recent months, there has been an escalation. Saudi Arabia was threatening Yemen to not break the blockade by operating a flight to Tehran, and as a response they bombed Sanaa Airport. And so since then, fighting has essentially escalated. Ansar Allah have now, as you said, taken over the entire west coast of Yemen. They had been controlling Bab el-Mandeb as you know, and there’s an active ceasefire between the United States and Ansar Allah since May of 2015 when they were blocking international shipping as a response to the genocide in Gaza. But now they fully control the coast and it’s very easy for them to disrupt shipping. But the key point here is that they’re not disrupting international shipping. They say that they are disrupting Saudi ships so that Saudi can finally lift the blockade on Yemen and not continue using Bab el-Mandeb Strait as they wish.

AMY GOODMAN: Can you explain the difference between the Yemeni government and the Houthis?

author: APTN National News
title: Ontario coroner announces inquest into death of Ojibwe man in Ottawa
content:
Ontario’s coroner says it will hold an inquest into the death of Gregory Ritchie, 30.


An Ojibway man from Saugeen First Nation in Ontario, Ritchie was shot and killed by Ottawa police on Jan. 31, 2019.


In February 2020,

Ontario’s Special Investigations Unit

 (SIU) announced that no charges would be laid against the officers.


According to the SIU report, police fired more than a dozen rounds at Ritchie, who held what appeared to be a tomahawk.


He was fatally hit by three bullets.


The director of the SIU, Joseph Martino, determined that “there are no reasonable grounds to lay criminal charges against any of the officers in relation to Mr. Ritchie’s death.”


Ritchie was reportedly walking to a pharmacy to pick up some medication.


Minutes before the pharmacy opened for the day, Ottawa police were called to the strip mall about a “suspicious incident” involving a man allegedly seen entering the building with a knife in his hand.


An altercation ensued, during which Ritchie was shot.


One of the officers reportedly received minor injuries.


Ritchie had recently moved to Ottawa from Kitchener, Ont. and was living with his brother and sister-in-law in the city’s south end.


An inquest is

mandatory under provincial law.


The coroner said details of the inquest will be announced at a later date.


The post

Ontario coroner announces inquest into death of Ojibwe man in Ottawa

 appeared first on

APTN News

.

author: Unknown
title: A New Issue of Inside Front : For Anarcho-Punks and Hardcore Anarchists
content:
Over three decades ago, some of the first people to collaborate on CrimethInc. projects met via the international networks that had developed in the zine underground associated with the

hardcore punk scene

. One of the first projects they collaborated on was the hardcore zine

Inside Front

, the archives of which are available

here

.


In those days, without the internet, how did people discover and pass on anarchist ideas and tactics?


By embedding these values in rebellious subcultural milieus such as the punk scene—by reading dogeared books about the Yippies, the Situationists, and the Spanish Civil War—and by having adventures.


These three elements—subculture, reading, and adventure—came together in the hardcore journal Inside Front.


The

last issue

 of

Inside Front

 came out in 2003.


In August 2025, as the hardcore band

Catharsis

 was preparing to play their first shows debuting their album “

Hope against Hope

,” the team behind

Inside Front

 suddenly came out of retirement and threw together a new issue of the magazine in a week flat.


As a consequences of some wrongheaded notions about authenticity and immediatism, the issue never appeared online, though Catharsis distributed them from New York City to Budapest.


Never, at least, until now.


We’ve added this

new issue of

Inside Front

 to our online archive, so you can print and distribute your own copies.


From the introduction:


We hastily prepared this special limited edition of Inside Front in just a few days, scrambling to finish it in time for the record release shows for the Catharsis LP “Hope against Hope.” Although it has been well over two
decades since the previous issue, many people who contributed to previous issues of Inside Front sent new material for this one—not to mention at least one contributor who was not yet born when the first issues of

Inside Front

 appeared.


Copies of the new issue of

Inside Front

 on a literature table in Budapest. This is like sighting a coelacanth in the wild.


From a

review

 by Martin on the

Counterforce

 site:


The cover says “For anarcho-punks and hardcore anarchists” and I could just stop the review right there. This might be the epitome of “perfect zine” for me. The first non-meta content is “Like Weeds – A Dialogue about HIS HERO IS GONE’s Timeless Anthem” in which two thinkers trade increasingly deep and heady observations and anecdotes about the song and it’s context (even more impressive when you realize both parties are almost certainly completely sober).


There’s also a relatable story about en EXTREME NOISE TERROR CD triggering scrutiny at the US border, a show review from someone’s first hardcore show ever, top-10 lists, a few reviews, ideas for a Stateless Fair, and a pair of parallel accounts from fighters in the Syrian civil war bonding over a Czechoslovakian hardcore song they all happened to know, and the struggle to finally download and listen to the song in the middle of a war zone.


It feels like a special and unique zine, since it draws on energy built up over 20+ years since the last issue. I’m not sure if Inside Front will return in a more permanent way, but I hope this issue gets wider distribution than just the CATHARSIS tour so more of you can enjoy it.


From the introduction to the zine:


Why hardcore, still, today, in the year 2025?


In the 1990s, in a time of social peace (at least in the United States), the hardcore scene was ahead of the times in that it was hyper-connected, internationally networked, and artistically experimental.


Today, the hardcore scene is increasingly conservative, artistically speaking (though we challenge you to prove us wrong!). It’s no longer any better networked than any other social milieu. But it is now old-fashioned in a potentially explosive way, because it involves physical collectivity, togetherness that unfolds on a slower time frame than the virtual reality of internet relations.


People have also become more aesthetically literate than they used to be. Whereas both a blast beat and a black bloc were completely foreign and incomprehensible to most people in 1999 (and both models derived both their strength and their limits from that fact), today, a much wider range of people can understand both of them. Yet as these reference points have become more widely shared, a crucial detail of the punk program has been lost: context is everything.

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: No Girls and women in Classrooms. No Women in Health Clinics. Afghanistan’s Healthcare Crisis Deepens by the Day.
content:
It has been five years since women and girls in Afghanistan have been among the primary targets of the Taliban regime. Their rights to go to school, go to work, and even leave their homes have been taken away. A direct consequence of these restrictions is a crumbling health system, under pressure from a lack of female medical professionals, Taliban restrictions, and funding cuts that threaten to keep health facilities open.

One of the first Taliban orders was to ban women from pursuing higher education and to ban all girls from attending school beyond grade six. According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls do not have access to education as a result of the Taliban’s ban. Other edicts target women’s freedom of movement, including restrictions that prevent women from leaving their homes or going to health clinics without a male family member. These edicts have built on one another to the point where Afghanistan’s education and health systems are being systematically dismantled. The pipeline that once supplied the workforce with trained and skilled professionals is disappearing, creating major long-term consequences for the health system and the country’s workforce.

Due to this dismantled pipeline, Afghanistan is facing one of the worst shortages of female medical professionals. In Helmand, Zabul, and Uruzgan provinces, it is reported that there are no female medical professionals. There are only three female specialists in Kandahar, a neighboring province to Helmand. In addition to specialists, other female healthcare workers that Afghanistan’s health system depends on, such as midwives and nurses, have been forced out of their jobs because of Taliban restrictions. And because of restrictions on movement, Afghan women are also unable to visit health facilities and obtain treatment, according to a February 2026 report by UN Special Rapporteur Richard Bennett.

The cost of the ban on education and the removal of women from the workforce also has a deep and lasting economic impact. It is estimated that this will cost Afghanistan $84 million per year. But beyond the economic impact, the immediate human consequences are even more urgent. Infant and maternal mortality have risen back to some of the highest levels seen since the Taliban took over.

The lack of specialists, and in some areas any female healthcare workers at all, means that women are facing a painful reality. An Afghan from Helmand shared, “We take patients from one doctor to another without success and eventually have to go elsewhere.”

Manizha, a medical doctor whose name has been changed for her safety, is part of one of the few medical teams still providing care to Afghan women. She sees women who would otherwise have no access to healthcare, with her team traveling to them. Her team originally started with fourteen members, but has since decreased to seven, as many of her colleagues were unable to find male guardians to accompany them to work, compounded by financial hardships.

With decreasing staff and an increasing health burden, the situation is dire. Even as Manizha faces enormous challenges, she remains hopeful: “Whenever I remember the smiles, the tears, and even the deprivation of the women I have visited over the years, I tell myself that I must not give up. They need even the little that I can do for them.”

Afghanistan’s healthcare system is collapsing because the foundation of a skilled labor force including women is collapsing. By excluding women from education, employment, and public life, the Taliban are not only denying women their rights today; they are dismantling the pipeline needed to train the healthcare professionals Afghanistan will need tomorrow. The result is a health system that is losing its existing female workforce while failing to produce the next generation of women professionals to serve their communities.

Sources: Feminist Majority Foundation, Afghanistan International, United Nations, UNICEF, Rukhshana

author: Saba Chaudhry
title: A popular movement in Kashmir defies severe repression
content:
This article

A popular movement in Kashmir defies severe repression

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


When activist Shahzaib Habib was killed by unidentified men on the night of June 6 in Rawalakot, Pakistan, protesters took custody of his body from the combined military hospital and staged a sit-in outside the hospital, demanding that an investigation be opened into his murder. Habib was a close associate of the leadership of the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee, or JAAC, a coalition of local traders, civil society members and political activists who spent the past three years organizing demonstrations across Pakistan-administered Kashmir. 


According to JAAC, security forces opened fire on the vehicle Habib was traveling in. Police say they intercepted a “suspicious vehicle” whose armed occupants fired first.


Habib’s killing came in a week when a crackdown on the JAAC was intensifying day by day. Two days earlier, on June 5, Pakistan’s government had banned JAAC, declaring the nonviolent coalition — which came together around electricity bills and wheat prices — a proscribed organization under the 2014 anti-terrorism act. In the days that followed, a curfew was imposed on Rawalakot, phone and internet were cut across the region of Azaad Jammu and Kashmir, and the government deployed the Pakistan Rangers, a paramilitary force. Protests were met

with violence

, leaving 11 dead. 


Previous Coverage


Kashmiri human rights defenders continue to fight injustices amid growing repression


Since the June 5 declaration, dozens of protesters have been arrested and many have reportedly been killed. But putting a precise number on either remains difficult. Media access to the region has been tightly restricted since the crackdown began, with phone and internet remaining suspended across much of the region.


Among those killed was one of the main student organizers: Usama Jamil, a PhD student at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad who was deputy secretary general of the Jammu Kashmir National Students Federation, or JKNSF. On July 27, according to student groups and civil society organizations, he was marching in Rawalakot, chanting for people’s rights, when he was shot and killed by security forces. 


The crackdown was not confined to Kashmir. Solidarity protests in Lahore, Islamabad and Karachi were met with arrests. In Lahore, police arrested activists and dozens of bystanders outside the press club during a peaceful demonstration on July 31. In Islamabad, the capital, 88 people were sent into 14-day judicial remand after a solidarity protest the same day. Human rights groups called the arrests part of a broader attempt to criminalize solidarity with Kashmir.


I asked Omer Khan, a member of JKNSF, about the current situation. “I don’t know how to answer this or where to begin,” he said. “A living hell was unleashed upon us, something this region has not witnessed in recent history. Our region was once one of the most peaceful, and now it has almost been turned into a war zone.”


“Dozens have been killed through direct state violence, and countless others have been injured,” he continued. “Food and medicine have been blocked. Frisking, raids and searches have violated the privacy and sanctity of people’s homes” and the entire region is under an undeclared curfew. 


He describes collective punishment as one of the more visible forms of state pressure, but says the psychological toll is harder to measure.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


But for now, despite the killings, crackdowns and internet restrictions, the movement the government tried to outlaw is still organizing. On Sept. 9, the JAAC led a region-wide shutter-down and wheel-jam strike, a form of general strike that aims to shut down all businesses and halt all road traffic. As of today, protesters remain in the streets. 


How the movement got there 


Organizers say that the keys to the movement’s durability have been its flat structure, the strong participation of women, and how it has built trust and solidarity by delivering victories that affect people’s everyday lives. 


“I consider it the world’s most modern and well-organized movement, and its biggest achievement is that it built solidarity among people,” said Haris Ahmed Khan, a member of Progressive Student Collective, or PSC, who was arrested at a peaceful solidary protest in Lahore on July 31 and later …

author: Zoë Yunker
title: Chinook are going blind on the Salmon River amid worsening drought conditions
content:
Over the summer, the Salmon River has slowed to a trickle, leaving fish in trouble in its warming waters. Photo courtesy of Secwépemc Fisheries Commission


This story originally appeared


in The Tyee


here

 and is reprinted with permission and minor style edits

.

It includes a photo of a Chinook salmon in distress that may be unsettling

 —

please look after your spirit and read with care.


In the Shuswap, Chinook salmon circle a small pool, preparing for the next leg of their journey up the Salmon River to spawn.


But this year, something is different: the salmon’s eyes have gone cloudy; some have fallen out entirely. The river they depend on has caused them to go blind.


For salmon, living conditions in the river are among the worst they’ve ever been. What was once a wide, cool waterway is now a thin, warm channel. Water can become a death trap, causing the fish to suffocate and sometimes lose vision. Blinded salmon are unlikely to live long enough to spawn.


In July, the province 

issued

 a protection order to limit irrigation throughout the region in the hope of reducing the destruction now underway. The order was 

rescinded

 less than two weeks later, with officials citing the interests of industrial water users intent on irrigating their crops as wildfires loomed. The order was then 

reissued

 on Aug. 19, after hundreds of chinook had arrived in the watershed.


Whether this year’s returning salmon will survive remains unclear.


Winding its way from the plateaus west of Okanagan Lake northeast to Shuswap Lake, the Salmon River is surrounded by intensive water users, including large ranches and farms. In recent years historically low levels of snowpack and precipitation have compounded those pressures, leading to unprecedented levels of water scarcity.


In the Salmon River, chinook salmon have gone blind over the summer because of deteriorating water conditions. Photo courtesy of Secwépemc Fisheries Commission


Orders restricting access to the Salmon River’s water have become an almost yearly occurrence as the region faces consecutive years of extreme drought. But this year’s first order came with an ominous distinction: stream flows were far lower than in any year previous, and the order came weeks earlier into the dry season.


Encoded in “B.C.’s” system of water laws, an emergency order is meant to be a last-ditch lever that authorities can pull when fish survival is at imminent risk. But in several watersheds they are now being used on a regular basis as the province faces ongoing drought.


Rosie Simms, director of place-based projects at the POLIS Water Sustainability Project at the University of Victoria, said the repeated use of orders is a sign that things need to change.


“We can’t be trying to fix drought in an emergency,” Simms said. She recently co-authored a 

report

 that documented patterns of prolonged drought across the province and called for a preventive approach to managing water in an era of increasing water scarcity.


“There’s a whole suite of things that would set us British Columbian communities up to be in a much better place to weather droughts and actually live well in drier conditions.”


In an email, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship wrote that “government has made preparing for drought conditions and responding to water scarcity a top priority, to safeguard the well-being of communities, businesses, ecosystems and wildlife.” They added that “the province is also working with partners on long-term, proactive solutions to improve water security in drought-prone watersheds.”


The water crisis in the southern Interior was anticipated long before the chinook began their journey upstream. In May, the Okanagan Nation Alliance 

declared

 a “watershed emergency” across rivers throughout the region, including the Salmon and Bessette watersheds.


The alliance of six Okanagan First Nations called for actions such as mandatory reductions in water use to protect fish flows and a co-governance forum between the syilx and the province to address water scarcity.


“Water is life, and the health of our watersheds can no longer be treated as secondary to development and short-term interests,” Westbank First Nation Chief Robert Louie said in a press release at the time.

author: Unknown
title: Repression and Resistance in Russia : An Overview
content:
Across three decades, Russia has been at the forefront of the worldwide

descent into authoritarianism

. Vladimir Putin’s government has suppressed opposition in ways that aspiring autocrats like Donald Trump are still striving to emulate. Yet despite widespread repression, there is still resistance in Russia, and as Putin’s model proliferates, people everywhere around the world stand to benefit from learning about it. Likewise, we should support Russian anarchist and

anti-war

 prisoners, both because resistance within Russia offers hope for the eventual end of war and totalitarianism and because, should autocrats consolidate power where we live, we will wish for people to support us, as well.


The following text is based on a presentation Antti Rautiainen offered at the

Baltic Anarchist Book Fair

 in Tartu on May 30, 2026. You can watch a video of the presentation

here

 or listen to it via

Spotify

.


In Russia, street protests against the war were crushed in 2022, the first year following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to the human rights organization

OVD Info

, 18,901 arrests for anti-war protests in year 2022 were followed by 274 arrests in 2023, 41 arrests in 2022, and just 13 arrests in first half of the year 2025. The reason for this sharp decline was the “Ilya Dadin” law of 2014, according to which “repeated offenses in following the established organization of protests” across a period of 180 days can result a prison sentence of up to 5 years. Thousands of people were arrested once or twice for taking part in anti-war street activities in 2022 and received either a fine or a prison sentence of a few days—but few risked being arrested for a third time.


Detentions for anti-war actions by year, first half of 2025, according to OVD-Info.


Russian polls have been unreliable since spring 2022. After the criminalization of anti-war opinions, some polling companies reported that up to 60% of people queried refused to give answers. Before the polls became unreliable, 58-71% of Russians indicated a pro-war sentiment in various polls. However, opinions were intensely polarized between different groups. People in major cities were more anti-war than those in other locations; younger people were more anti-war, as were women. The greatest division was between people who watch television, the chief propaganda tool of the state, and people who do not watch it. Among people less than 30 years old who do not watch television,

80% were anti-war

.


The general impression among critical Russians is that the majority of those in Russia still share a pro-war sentiment. However, a shift is visible even in officially tolerated opinion polls. According to polls by the

Levada Center

, over the past two years, the share of Russians supporting the continuation of the war effort has dropped from around 41% to around 28%, and share of those who support peace talks has grown from 51% to 62%. At the same time, the number of those who support making concessions to Ukraine is at 24%: people want peace, but on terms favorable to Russia.


Of course, this may simply reflect what people are willing to say to anonymous pollsters.


Another difference is that now, people in small cities and rural localities are expressing more anti-war sentiment than those in major urban centers. Moscow is the most pro-war city. The likely explanation is that most of the frontline casualties are from small, peripheral communities.


Factors Undermining the Anti-War Movement


Why, after more than four years of war, with more than a million Russian soldiers wounded or dead, is anti-war sentiment still confined to a minority?


As the saying goes, “It’s the economy, stupid.” During the first years of the war, salaries were growing even with high inflation rate. Starting in 2004, the Russian ruling class hoarded huge profits of the oil and gas trade in a fund currently known as the “National Wealth Fund.” Instead of raising the standard of living by investing in healthcare, social benefits and services, and the like, the money was stashed to be spent on wars and militarization. Now these billions are finally flowing into the economy in the form of wartime investment. The unemployment rate is negligible; in some cases, salaries have multiplied at factories in regions that were previously economically depressed. Generous monthly payments for contract soldiers are up to five times the average salary in poorer regions. At the same …

author: C4SS
title: Attacco alla Libertà Tecnologica e al Dissenso
content:
C4SS

. Pubblicato l’otto settembre 2026 con il titolo

An Attack on Tech Freedom, an Assault on Dissent

. Traduzione di

Enrico Sanna

.


Viviamo in un mondo caratterizzato da

stato di polizia

,

militarizzazione della polizia

, e

repressione


del


dissenso

. Con i colossi aziendali spesso alleati con lo stato per

mettere a tacere chi dissente

 o per rafforzare la

sorveglianza

.


Dato il contesto, è importante che i gruppi autonomi abbiano piattaforme di comunicazione e hosting criptate.


Per aver fatto ciò, un collettivo italiano è stato recentemente

dichiarato

 “associazione terroristica globale” dall’amministrazione Trump. Il collettivo è Autistici/Inventati, che offre servizi ad attivisti tramite il servizio di hosting

NoBlogs

 e altre infrastrutture digitali.


Secondo

 il dipartimento di stato degli Stati Uniti, “Autistici/Inventati (A/I) è un gruppo estremista con base in Italia che crea e gestisce infrastrutture digitali al servizio di cellule antifasciste (antifa) violente e gruppi militanti di estrema sinistra in tutto il mondo”.


L’accento sulle

cellule antifasciste

 riflette il tentativo in corso dell’amministrazione Trump di abbattere il dissenso demonizzando gli “antifascisti”. Questo è l’obiettivo esplicito del memorandum presidenziale sulla sicurezza nazionale (

NSPM-7

), ed è alla base delle azioni penali contro gli attivisti anti-CIE (che gestisce i rimpatri), come

Minneapolis 15

 e

Prairieland defendants

.


Nel loro desiderio ossessivo di collegare tutto il dissenso anarchico e di sinistra agli “antifascisti”, l’amministrazione Trump è incorsa in dichiarazioni sfacciatamente false. Così il dipartimento di stato:


L’organizzazione antifascista Rose City, con base nell’Oregon, si è servita di strutture e servizi del collettivo A/I per coordinare e spingere a compiere localmente atti violenti e criminali, compreso un attacco contro gli elicotteri della polizia di frontiera che ha portato ad una denuncia federale. Rose City si è inoltre servita di strumenti e servizi di A/I per diffondere liste di proscrizione e informazioni personali ottenute illegalmente sulla polizia di frontiera, oltre a inviti a prendere di mira agenti in strada e “in casa loro”.


Ma come

fa notare

 la rete antifascista Torch, Rose City non è responsabile di tali azioni e non si serve di A/I. Gli agenti federali si riferiscono ai comunicati di Rose City Counter-Info, un’organizzazione completamente diversa che fa uso dei servizi di A/I. “Rose City” è un appellativo molto comune a Portland, nell’Oregon. Il nome accomuna organizzazioni diverse tra loro. Si tratta di chiare falsità ingenuamente amplificate da giornalisti di

Fox News

 e

National Review

.


Al di là dell’incompetenza dimostrata, dire che il collettivo A/I è una “associazione terroristica globale” è, questa sì, una minaccia serissima. Come

afferma

 il coordinatore tecnico di C4SS William Gillis, “È un FORTE attacco contro il diritto elementare di libertà di parola. Non oso immaginare quale colpo potrebbe subire un movimento anarchico costituito, come dicono gli Stati Uniti, da 5.500 mailing list e 10.000 blog.”


Il dipartimento di stato punta il dito contro gli utenti dei servizi di A/I accusandoli di aver commesso presunti reati, come il sabotaggio e il terrorismo. Ma si tratta perlopiù di attività che rientrano chiaramente nel primo emendamento (libertà di parola, religione, stampa e assemblea,

NdT

). Ci rientrano l’organizzazione di fiere del libro anarchico, attività di ricerca antifascista che studiano e denunciano organizzazioni di estrema destra e anche il blog di una rivista accademica di revisione paritaria e una trasmissione radio con podcast anarchico.


Classificare A/I come “associazione terroristica globale” significa a sanzioni. Significa che chiunque faccia transazioni con A/I si espone a rappresaglie legali, e questo sulla base di un decreto dell’esecutivo. Il risultato è che il sito del collettivo è stato

chiuso

,

PayPal

 ha bloccato il conto e lo stesso conta di fare l’italiana

Banca Etica

,


Si tratta di sanzioni che hanno un effetto devastante per A/I.

Così


Sabot Media

: “Il sei settembre, undici giorni dopo che gli Stati Uniti hanno messo il collettivo italiano nell’elenco delle attività terroristiche, A/I ha annunciato che chiuderà, tutti i servizi di email, blogging, hosting e comunicazioni offerti da venticinque anni saranno interrotti.”


Un precedente agghiacciante. Il governo può …
